newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asian Metal-Demand slow, aluminium seen vulnerable.
newsitem.headline: Asian Metal-Demand slow, aluminium seen vulnerable.

text.p: Asian base metal demand will probably remain sluggish ahead of the Chinese New Year while a surge in aluminium prices in the London Metal Exchange (LME) may be cut short by profit-taking, metal traders said on Friday.
"With the Chinese New Year coming up soon, (base metal) demand is going to be slow," the director of a Japanese metal trading company told Reuters.

"Asian base metal demand is not so good," a dealer for a Japanese trading house added. "With many economies in the region so sluggish, demand in the appliance and car manufacturing sectors has gone down."
He said aluminium producers, for instance, have large inventories which they would have to trim by up to 20 percent in the first quarter of 1997.
"We should see a pickup after the New Year holidays," the trader said. The Chinese Lunar New Year will be celebrated on February 7 and 8.
A senior dealer at a European metal trading company said buying for copper in the region has become soft, especially since China has ample stocks.
"Normally, you should see the Chinese come into the market to buy before the New Year. But they have enough material available to meet their needs," the dealer said.
Several dealers dismissed the recent strong gains in LME base metal prices as largely driven by investment funds.
Three month aluminium, which hit a seven month high in the LME on Thursday of US$1,610 a tonne, may be vulnerable to profit-taking this afternoon or early next week, they said.
Copper has also benefitted from the surge, with three-month prices closing in late trade on the LME on Thursday at $2,270/74 a tonne.

"Aluminium may go up to $1,620, but that's it. I don't think it has the strength to remain above $1,600," a chartist for a Singapore-based metal trading firm said. He said it could slide all the way back to $1,580 a tonne.
"It's totally fund-driven," another dealer said. "We seem to be in a technical buying spree at the moment. It's really a question of how long the funds will buy into the market."
The LME is vulnerable to a fund-driven rally because the base metal trade still has to find its footing, one dealer said.
"That's why the funds are pushing the market around. It's so early in the year and the trade is still trying to decide what to do," he said.
A Japanese trader added: "The market may rise a bit further, but you could see a correction."

Three-month aluminium prices were quoted in Singapore at $1,606/11 a tonne at 0430 GMT, unchanged from the level at 0245 GMT, metal dealers said. They also quoted three month copper at $2,268/73 a tonne at 0430 GMT.
Cash copper was seen at 0430 GMT at $2,413/18 a tonne with backwardation at about $145, the traders said.
Base metal premiums over LME cash prices in the city-state also remained soft due to the presence of ample supplies of material here, the traders said.
Copper premiums were treading between $10-$25 a tonne and the expected arrival of anywhere from 2,000 to 10,000 tonnes in Singapore soon will probably depress premiums further, dealers said.
The amount of copper in the LME's Singapore warehouse climbed to 39,750 tonnes on Tuesday, an increase of 9,850 tonnes from the previous report on January 3.
Aluminium defied the bearish tone of premium prices with Western material being quoted at about $75 a tonne against a quote late last year of $60-$70 a tonne.
"People are still trying to charge the high premiums for aluminium, but no one's interested," one dealer said.
